- **① The version marker named someone else's release (major).** The branch stamped `2.369.61` into 36 places across 17 files while master had ALREADY SHIPPED `2.369.61` (Alt+Enter = steer) — 16 seconds before this branch's own commit. Same class as the 2.369.58 r2 renumber off `2.369.54`. Renumbered to **2.369.62** in one pass. The belt that existed (test-harness-honesty's CHANGELOG rule) could not see it: a branch that is not rebased has no CHANGELOG entry for EITHER number, so the check passes vacuously. **The number is claimed on the INTEGRATION BRANCH, so the check has to ask git** — leg ⑩ scans `origin/master`'s release-commit subjects AND its CHANGELOG headings for the marker and fails unless the claimant IS this change, with the old number `2.369.61` as a standing negative control (it must still read as claimed-by-someone-else, or the check is blind). No ref ⇒ explicit SKIP, never a silent pass.
- **② `effortNext: null` is a statement, not a gap (minor).** The new session-meta writer read `payload.effortNext || payload.effort` — re-conflating the two facts the release exists to separate. Picking "Auto (model default)" makes the wrapper clear the thread's effort and publish `{effort:'<the last turn ran at>', effortNext:null}`; the fallback then wrote the last turn's LEVEL into `session._effort`, session-meta, the attach payload's `chatStatus.effortNext`, the chip after a restart and the next resume spawn — overwriting the `null` ws-handler had just written on the same click. Now `effortNext` is the only field read, and only when present (`undefined` = an old wrapper says nothing ⇒ master's behaviour, the 2.361.1/2.364.1 skew rule).
- **③ A record in codex's spelling that codex refused (minor).** `set-effort` emitted `thread_settings_applied` — codex's OWN rollout shape — unconditionally, including after `thread/settings/update` was rejected, and unmarked. Our payload carries 5 `thread_settings` keys where codex's real one carries 9 (`model_provider_id`, `approvals_reviewer`, `collaboration_mode`, `permission_profile`…), so the two can never share a fingerprint and a rebuilt history kept both forever. Now: recorded only when the RPC was ACCEPTED (a refusal leaves the per-turn `turn/start` fallback, and the pending pick still reaches every client through `wrapper_meta.effortNext` — a statement about US, which a refusal leaves true), and both wrapper-authored copies carry `wrapper: true` like the synthesized `turn_context`. `mergeCodexRecords` folds the twin the same way (codex's copy wins), keyed on the stated VALUES and scoped to ADJACENCY — high → ultra → high is a real sequence, and folding the third into the first would leave a rebuilt status reporting `ultra`.
- **④ The disclosed resume gap needed an owner, not a paragraph (minor).** Filed as B-6b6d with the MODEL twin; scope corrected above.

**Round-2 invariants.** ⑥ A version marker is a CROSS-REFERENCE: it must resolve on the branch it will be integrated into, and the only source that knows is git — a CHANGELOG check on an un-rebased branch is vacuous by construction. ⑦ `null` from a producer that always sends the field is a VALUE ("nothing pending"); only `undefined` is absence. Never `a || b` across two fields that mean different things — that is the exact conflation the incident is about, re-introduced one layer down. ⑧ Never write a record in another party's spelling for something that party did not do; if you must synthesize one, MARK it, and let the real author's copy win the fold.

Gate: scripts/test-codex-effort-meta.mjs (108) — the race reproduced against a stub app-server with the REAL wrapper, plus per-defect regression legs with negative controls (master's own record shapes; a REFUSING app-server; `effortNext:null` vs an old wrapper's absent field; adjacent-vs-sequential settings twins; the squatted version number).
## B-7638 — THE SEVEN REVIEW RESIDUALS (the 2026-09-06 review-fixes-r2 verify; every one reproduced before it was fixed)

Three fixes shipped in that batch each left something behind that the verify pass named and the repro confirmed. They are unrelated in code and identical in shape: **a rule was written for the state the incident happened to be in, and the state it drifts into afterwards was never asked about.**

**① The over-cap adoption trusted a 4 KB window (src/hosts.js).** The remote-transcript cache heals a pre-provenance slot by refetching it whole, with ONE exception: a remote already past `maxBytes` cannot be refetched at all, so a byte-verified cache adopts the provenance instead of failing "too large". "Byte-verified" read the last 4 KB — sound at the moment of a splice, because an append lands its foreign bytes at the TAIL. But the pre-fix delta path kept appending AFTER it spliced, so on any long-lived slot the marker is buried under later appends and a tail read calls the hybrid verified — forever, because a stopped thread never changes again. The whole-file scan (1 MiB chunks, 3-byte carry so a zstd magic split across a boundary is still seen) is the evidence such a slot owes. **Round 2 corrected WHICH slots owe it.** The first cut gated the deep scan on "the meta carries no `remotePath`" — but that is exactly the provenance the *shipped* tail-only adoption used to stamp: it adopted a buried hybrid and the delta path then wrote `remotePath` onto that very slot, so `sameRemote` is TRUE for the corruption the scan exists to find, and every slot that passed through the ⑥ window would have been served on a tail check forever. The gate is now a meta SCHEMA MARKER (`v: 2`) written by every meta writer in `_fetchRemoteByFind`: any meta from before this fix pays ONE whole-file scan the first time its bytes are trusted, and is re-stamped so the cost is paid once per slot, never per poll. A refused slot is left unstamped.

**① b The cap error's remediation could not work (src/hosts.js).** The same batch appended "delete it to re-sync" to the "too large" error when the cache did not verify. The suffix is reachable ONLY when the remote is past the cap — where a whole refetch is impossible by construction — so following the advice destroyed the last local copy and failed identically (verified: delete cache → same error; delete cache AND meta → same error). It now states the true situation: no prefix to grow from, the remote is past the *N* MB cap, and deleting the cache would not help. Advice in an error message is a claim about the system; it needs the same evidence as any other claim.

**② The ssh rung could not grow an over-cap slot (src/hosts.js).** Both early-return branches handed the verified cache back and left the meta unstamped, so the whole-file scan repeated on every poll; `stampVerified` (remotePath + compressed + `adopted` + the schema marker) on both rungs ends that — **and that is all the stamp does**. The round-2 verify caught the first cut claiming more: the *harm* here was that the legacy ssh rung hard-failed "remote transcript too large" on the very next byte of growth, and stamping provenance changes nothing on that path (the short-circuit needs `meta.size === size`, so any growth falls straight into the cap throw, with no fallback to the verified cache — a >64 MB transcript that opened yesterday was an error today). The real fault was a TWIN GAP: the slab rung has grown an over-cap slot by an append-only delta since 2.187.0 and the ssh rung only ever whole-`cat`ted, so the same conversation behaved differently depending on which transport happened to serve it. The ssh rung now carries the same delta (`tail -c +N`, 1-based on GNU and BSD), under the same legality test (same remote file, uncompressed on both sides, cached prefix no longer than the remote) and the same never-stamp-bytes-we-did-not-get rule — with one refinement the last rung needs: a read that OVERTAKES the stat (a live transcript grew mid-poll) keeps the extra bytes, because an append-only file's extra tail bytes are genuinely its next bytes, and stamps what the cache actually holds; only a SHORT read throws.

**② b ROUND 3 — the three residuals of the round-2 delta itself (src/hosts.js).** The verify that passed round 2 named them, and each was reproduced before it was fixed.
  **(i) The compression-legality clause had no negative control on either rung.** `canDelta`/`canDeltaSsh` both carry `!isZstPath(remotePath) && !cacheIsCompressed()`, and DELETING it left test-codex-zst ALL PASS — the suite only ever exercised the twin-SWITCH (plain ⇄ .zst), never a growth with BOTH sides compressed. That case is the innocent-looking one and the worst: a host re-compresses a finished rollout, so the remote keeps its path, the cache holds .zst bytes that verify (for a compressed slot the magic IS the evidence), and the cached archive is shorter than the remote — every other delta precondition holds. The "delta" would weld a foreign frame tail onto the old frames; `zstdDecompressFrames` then stops at the earlier frames and the slot serves the OLD transcript, with the growth silently gone. Both rungs now carry a both-compressed growth leg (⑥d) whose asserts go red when the clause is deleted from EITHER copy — the two legality tests are twins, and a guard only one copy carries is the drift this batch keeps paying for.
  **(ii) The delta REPLACED the last rung's whole `cat`.** Round 2 added `tail -c +N` to the ssh rung as an `if/else` against the whole-`cat` branch, so a `tail` that FAILS — the remote truncated/rotated between the stat and the read, or a host whose `tail` has no `-c +N` — now hard-fails a fetch the pre-r2 code completed, and this is the LAST rung: nothing under it to fall through to. A delta failure now falls back to the whole `cat` when `size <= maxBytes` (logging the failure VERBATIM, per the degrade-path rule), and the hard error is kept ONLY over the cap — where a whole re-pull is impossible by construction and the delta really was the only road, so the fallback can never become a cap bypass. The over-cap short-read hard failure from round 2 is unchanged.
  **(iii) The meta writers rebuilt provenance instead of carrying it.** Both rungs stamped a FRESH object at the end of a fetch, so the very next delta erased `adopted` (the marker meaning "these bytes were VERIFIED, never fetched") and the `slab` lane marker — the exact opposite of the durability ① claims, and it landed on the one slot class that can never re-earn it (an over-cap slot cannot be refetched to prove itself again). One shared `nextMeta(fields, {whole})` now spreads the prior meta on BOTH rungs; only a WHOLE refetch clears those two markers, because they describe bytes that are no longer in the slot.

**② c ROUND 4 — TWO POLLS, ONE SLOT, ONE OFFSET (src/hosts.js).** Both rungs are now read-then-append against a size measured BEFORE the remote read, and nothing serialized the SLOT. Two overlapping fetches of the same conversation — the 5s session poll and a user opening the window, two clients, goal-sync and an attach — each read `fs.statSync(cachePath).size`, each asked the host for `[localSize, size)`, and each appended it: the cache grew a DUPLICATED region. That much self-heals (a doubled file no longer matches its own meta ⇒ whole refetch), which is why three review passes walked past it; the permanent damage is one poll later. Once the remote grows past the doubled size the legality test holds again, the next tail is appended at the doubled offset, and the file's size now EQUALS the remote's — so the stamp says COMPLETE and the short-circuit serves it forever, with a region duplicated and the region behind it MISSING. Nothing catches it downstream either: duplicated JSON records carry neither a NUL byte nor a zstd magic, so the byte checks of ① are silent, and a stopped conversation never changes again. Two independent legs, because the failure has two independent sources. **(i) The slot is single-flighted**: `_fetchRemoteByFind` is now a thin wrapper over the core (`_fetchRemoteByFindOnce`) holding an in-flight promise per cache path — a second caller AWAITS the first's verdict instead of racing it (one remote read, one append; every caller resolves its cap from the same harness descriptor, so a coalesced caller cannot lose a cap it needed, and the next poll re-decides with its own). **(ii) The append refuses a stale offset**: `_appendDeltaAt(cachePath, offset, buf)` opens `r+`, re-reads the size THROUGH the fd it is about to write with, and writes POSITIONALLY at `offset` — at a matching offset the write is idempotent, at a mismatching one it does not happen at all. `false` means "the slot moved": under the cap that is a whole refetch on both rungs (the ssh rung reuses the round-3 fallback), over the cap — where a whole re-pull is impossible by construction — it is a loud failure that leaves the slot exactly as it was found. Pins: test-codex-zst ⑥f, with pre-fix repros for both legs (the doubling, then the poll that seals it and the short-circuit that then serves it forever) and mutation-tested one leg at a time: deleting the single-flight reddens the two coalescing asserts on both rungs, deleting the offset check reddens the four moved-slot asserts.

**② d ROUND 5 — THE REFUSAL THAT DEGRADED (src/hosts.js).** Round 4's moved-slot refusal was correct and unreachable on the rung that needed it most. The over-cap `throw` sits INSIDE the data-plane `try`, and that catch means "this TRANSPORT did not work, try the other one" — so on a dial host (or any host with the data plane on) with a reachable ssh fallback the refusal landed in `catch (e2) { /* legacy fallback below */ }`, silently, and the ssh rung then measured `fs.statSync(cachePath).size` on the MOVED file, computed a fresh tail offset from it and appended: the remote's bytes for the moved region were never fetched, the file's size nevertheless EQUALS the remote's, the meta stamps COMPLETE, and a stopped conversation serves the hole forever. Reproduced verbatim (dial transport, foreign 203-byte append during `fsReadRange`, remote past the cap): no error, no log line, `meta.size == remote size`, remote bytes [P, P+203) missing — and the next poll short-circuited on it. Three legs, each mutation-tested alone. **(i) The verdict is typed.** `slotMovedError` carries `code:'ESLOTMOVED'` and the catch re-throws it (`_isTerminalFetchError`): a statement about the CACHE is true on every rung; only TRANSPORT failures may degrade. **(ii) What a rung learned outlives it.** `observed.moved` (`_slotMovedEarlier`) denies the ssh rung a delta even when the slab rung reached the fallback for an unrelated reason — it can observe the movement, refetch whole UNDER the cap, and then have that whole read die on the wire. **(iii) The durable half.** One poll later the movement is invisible to `_appendDeltaAt`: the foreign bytes are simply in the file, the offset it re-reads MATCHES them, and the append lands right behind them — so the fix would only have delayed the corruption by one poll. `_prefixIsOurs(localSize, meta)` asks the meta instead of the clock: a delta may extend only bytes this cache's own writers stamped (the file may not hold MORE than `meta.size`). A SHORTER file stays growable on purpose — a positional append only ever writes at the end, so a short file is still a genuine prefix (a crash between the append and the meta write, a truncation), and refusing it would strand every over-cap slot that ever crashed mid-write. Over the cap every one of these is a loud failure that leaves cache AND meta byte-identical, and the cap error names WHICH fault it is ("could not be verified" vs "holds N bytes where the last fetch stamped M"). Two consequences fell out: the whole `cat` now stamps `buf.length` instead of the stat it was promised (a live transcript hands back more bytes than the probe said — the tail branch of the same rung has always stamped the real length, and an under-claiming meta would make (iii) read our own fetch as foreign bytes), and the data-plane catch now LOGS every fault it swallows VERBATIM — it logged nothing at all, which is how a degrade path hides a lost binding for three days (2.340.2).

**② e ROUND 6 — THE SHAPE ROUND 5 CONDEMNED BY MISTAKE (src/hosts.js).** Round 5's "grow only what we stamped" is right about foreign appends and wrong about one INNOCENT shape it cannot tell apart from them. Until round 5 the whole `cat` rung stamped the PROBE's stat while `cat` returned everything the live transcript had grown to since, so a perfectly healthy fetch left `meta.size` SHORTER than the file it wrote. Under the cap that costs one whole re-pull and heals; OVER the cap there is no whole re-pull, so `_prefixIsOurs` turned every such slot — a remote stopped thread that opened yesterday — into a permanent hard failure ("holds N bytes where the last fetch stamped M"), forever, because nothing on either side can ever move again. The heal cannot be a local scan: the corruption round 5 exists for appends ORDINARY TEXT (⑥g/E2), which no NUL/magic/record-boundary check can distinguish from our own missing bytes. So the only witness that can tell them apart is asked — THE REMOTE. When a slot is over the cap AND its meta predates the `sizeExact` marker AND the file is longer than that meta claims, the gap `[stamp, file)` is read back (a BOUNDED read of just the gap: `fsReadRange` on the slab rung, `tail -c +N | head -c LEN` on the ssh one) and compared byte-for-byte with what the cache holds there. Equal ⇒ genuine prefix, the stamp was merely short ⇒ re-stamp `meta.size = file size` with the marker, ONCE, and the delta rides again. Not equal ⇒ round 5's refusal stands, unchanged. Four bounds keep it from becoming a way around round 5 or a per-poll cost: only over the cap (under it a whole refetch is the remedy — adopting bytes you can simply re-fetch is trusting what you did not have to trust), only for marker-less metas (a round-5+ writer stamps what the file holds, so a longer file THERE is genuinely foreign), never on a slot a rung watched move in this window (`_slotMovedEarlier` — we already know where those bytes came from), and free local evidence FIRST (the round-3 whole-file splice scan, skipped when this poll's `cacheUsable` already paid for it). The verification is written to disk the moment it is PROVEN, not when the fetch that triggered it finishes — otherwise a delta that dies on the wire throws the proof away and the next poll pays again, on exactly the slots where the fetch is least likely to complete. A refusal, by contrast, is memoized IN MEMORY only (per slot, keyed by the size it was made on, 10 min): stamping a slot we would not serve freezes the corruption in, and the memo also carries the VERDICT so the replayed refusal gives the same diagnosis. Four verdicts, four different sentences appended to the cap error — a checked byte mismatch, a splice marker found locally, a slot seen moving, and "the remote could not be read (retryable)" — because a refusal that claims the check it skipped is "an error string is not a diagnosis" with the sign flipped. Second half, the round-5 MINOR's own cost: the degrade line round 5 added is now rate-limited per HOST (≤1/60s, `_warnDegradeOnce`, carrying `(+N similar suppressed…)` onto the next window) — the thing it degrades on is usually persistent, and every attach/poll/goal-sync tick comes through there, so a line per fetch is a journal that says one sentence.

**② f ROUND 7 — THE HEAL'S OWN COSTS, AND A GUARD THAT NEVER ASKED WHAT IT WAS COMPARING (src/hosts.js).** The round-6 verify named three, each reproduced before it was fixed. **(i) "Paid once per slot" was paid twice per poll, every poll.** The whole-file splice scan is a SYNCHRONOUS read of the entire cache file on the event loop, and round 6's own comment claimed it was "skipped when this poll's `cacheUsable` already paid for it" — true only within ONE rung. `cacheUsable` runs on the slab rung, the slab rung's "too large" is degradable, so the ssh rung runs it again: two whole reads of a 64 MB slot per poll. And "per poll" is the worse half — the slots that owe the scan are exactly the ones that REFUSE, and a refused poll leaves the meta byte-identical BY DESIGN (round 6's disk invariant), so nothing ever retires the legacy marker: every session poll, window attach and goal-sync tick re-read the whole file, forever. The verdict is a statement about BYTES, so it is now memoized against the bytes it was made on — the cache file's identity (inode, size, mtime), 10 min TTL, dropped explicitly by every writer in the fetch that touches the slot. That makes it free across rungs AND across polls, so the `deepDone` flag is gone: the heal asks the question outright instead of inferring from a flag whether some earlier caller happened to have answered it. The scan itself now answers in THREE states — clean / a marker is in there / the file could not be read — because only a VERDICT may be remembered: the caller refuses the poll either way, but memoizing an unreadable file would let a transient EMFILE freeze a healthy slot for the whole TTL (the same line round 6 drew between a refusal and 'unverified'). Invariant: **a "paid once" claim is about a CACHE, and a cache needs a key that names what it is about — the flag that says "someone already did this" is only true inside the scope that set it.** **(ii) A rate limiter that suppressed the wrong thing.** Round 6's `_warnDegradeOnce` keyed the 60 s window on the HOST id alone, so the first fault held the whole minute and a DIFFERENT fault on that host inside it — the heal's gap probe dying while the link flaps, a free identifier an extraction left behind (the 2.340.2 class this line exists to expose) — was dropped into a "+N similar" tally that names nothing: the rate limiter became the silent catch it replaced. "Similar" has to MEAN similar, so the window is keyed on the host AND the message's CLASS (`_degradeClassKey`: the same sentence with its offsets/sizes/ids blanked). Each distinct fault speaks once a minute; only genuine repeats are counted. **(iii) The gap comparison never asked whether it was still the file it measured.** The heal compares the cache's `[stamp, EOF)` with the remote's own bytes, and the two sides are taken at DIFFERENT times: `localSize` from a stat before the remote round trip, the local bytes after it. A slot that shrinks in between (a truncation, a non-atomic writer, an operator repairing it) hands back a short region, and the pre-fix code read that mismatch as the strongest verdict it has — 'foreign' ("the bytes past that point were CHECKED against the remote: they are not its own") — and MEMOIZED it for ten minutes, so one transient shrink condemned a perfectly healthy over-cap slot and the memo replayed the mis-diagnosis on every later poll with no probe left to correct it. `_healGapIsStillOurs` (neuterable, like every other leg here) re-stats before comparing: a slot that changed under the probe is the MOVED class — terminal for this poll, remembered by nobody, re-judged next poll. Invariant: **a comparison between two reads taken at different times must prove they are about the same object before it may report the DIFFERENCE as evidence — and a fact about a race may never be memoized as a fact about the bytes.** Pins: test-codex-zst (M)/(N)/(O) — the pre-fix scan count (3, then +2 per poll) against one scan for the slot over three polls and two rungs, plus memo-cleared and bytes-changed negative controls; both key shapes A/B'd on the same two faults; the shrink race reproduced as a memoized 'foreign' that survives the file's recovery, then as a shifted verdict whose very next poll heals the slot.

**③ A transcript shorter than the magic could never be verified (src/hosts.js).** `head.length < 4 ⇒ refetch` meant an empty or one-record transcript was fully re-pulled on EVERY poll, forever. A cache under 4 bytes cannot BE a zstd frame and cannot hide a splice: it verifies (still subject to "a .jsonl cache starts with a record"), while a sub-magic cache under a COMPRESSED remote is still refused.

**④ A home-dir dot glob widened to every user (src/plugin-manifest.js).** 2.369.44 taught the validator that node reads a declared fs path only up to the first `*` and grants by STRING PREFIX; 2.369.43 taught it to collapse `.` segments the way node does. At `~/.*` the two rules collide: node keeps `.*` as an ordinary segment (the grant is the prefix `<home>/.` — dotfiles), but collapsing the dot HERE emitted `<home>*` — the whole home directory plus every sibling path starting with those characters (`/home/u*` reaches `/home/u2/…`). The manifest said one thing and node was handed another, invisibly. A `.` segment immediately before `*` is now refused, naming the prefix it would have produced.

**⑤–⑦ The ACP bookkeeping nudge is OURS, not the user's (data/bin/acp-wrapper.js).** Three consequences of one confusion:
  ⑤ The 'queue-cleared' notice ("send it again") subtracted dropped NUDGE entries but not dropped PEER ones — and a peer message is not the user's to re-send either: it goes back to the delivery ladder on `peer_result ok:false` and arrives again on its own, so the advice was both wrong and impossible to follow. Nudges AND peers are subtracted now; the log line keeps the true total.
  ⑥ The nudge queued with a visible `queued_input`, painting a "Queued" chip on a bubble that does not exist. It queues with `silentQueue` (as peer messages already did) and stays visible in `queue_changed` as kind 'system', so the strip is still honest about what is waiting.
  ⑦ **A Stop landing inside the `/api/agent/stop-check` round trip still billed a turn.** The nudge is fetched by `endPrompt` and dispatched when the answer lands — by then the interrupt has finished and `activePrompt` is null, so the fetch resolved straight into `runPrompt` and started a fresh turn the user had just asked to stop; the only trace was a reminder appearing out of nowhere. The interrupt now bumps `stopEpoch` and aborts the request in flight, and an answer whose epoch is gone is discarded with a logged reason. The latch is never set on that path, so the NEXT completed turn nudges normally.

**INVARIANTS.** (a) A verification window sized for the moment of corruption expires the moment anything is appended after it — a decision that ADOPTS unverified bytes must pay for evidence over the whole artifact, and record that it did so, so the cost is paid once. (a2) That record must be a marker THIS code writes (a schema version), never a field the buggy code also wrote: gating a heal on "the old code left this blank" misses every slot the old code filled in on its way past the bug — and a fix's own release window is where those slots come from. (a3) Name the harm the fix removes, then prove the fix removes THAT: a change that is separately correct ("record the adoption") can be shipped with a false causal claim attached ("…so growth syncs"), and a test that quietly relaxes the condition under test (dropping `maxBytes` on the growth poll) will agree with it. (a4) Advice inside an error message is a claim about the system — if the branch that emits it can only be reached where the advice cannot work, it is a false claim, not a courtesy. (a5) A guard nobody can delete-and-fail is not a guard: every legality clause owes a leg that goes RED when that clause alone is removed — and when the clause exists in twin form on two rungs, it owes one on EACH, or the copies drift the moment one is edited. (a6) A fast path added under an existing one must leave the slow path REACHABLE: replacing the only road with an optimisation turns every failure mode of the optimisation into a failure of the whole feature, and on the LAST rung there is nothing below to catch it — fall back where the slow path is still possible, and hard-fail only where it provably is not. (a7) A meta writer overwrites what it just LEARNED, never what it inherited: durable provenance and a fresh object literal are contradictory designs, and the field that gets erased is always the one that cannot be re-earned. (a8) A read-then-write against a size measured before the read is a lost update waiting for a second caller: serialize the RESOURCE (the cache slot), and make the write itself refuse the offset it was computed from once that offset is no longer the end of the file — a positional write at a re-checked offset is idempotent where a blind append is a duplicated region. Corollary for the repro: a duplication whose records are IDENTICAL is byte-identical to the correct file, so a fixture built from repeated records will pass the negative control while the bug is fully present. (a9) **A refusal is only a refusal on the rung that can be reached.** A guard thrown inside a try whose catch degrades to another implementation is not a guard — it is a slower path to the same corruption, because the fallback re-derives its inputs from the very state the guard refused to trust. Classify the throw: a TRANSPORT failure may degrade, a verdict about the shared RESOURCE must be terminal on every rung and must travel as a CODE the fallback tests, never as a message nobody reads. (a10) **A guard that only sees the race window has to be paired with one that reads the evidence the race left behind.** An in-window check (re-read the offset through the fd you are about to write with) expires the moment the poll ends: next time round, the foreign bytes are simply part of the file and every in-window question answers "fine". The durable form asks a record the code wrote itself — grow only what we stamped — which also means every writer must stamp what the file ACTUALLY holds, or the invariant starts reading our own fetches as foreign. Corollary: when a fix's negative control needs three separate neuterings to reproduce the original bug, that is not redundancy to trim — it is three independent legs, and the suite should be able to remove each one alone and go red. (a11) **A rule written for a corruption will also condemn every innocent shape that wears the same signature — find them before shipping it, because the rule's own remedy may not exist for them.** "The file holds more than we stamped" is foreign bytes AND our own short stamp, and the branch where a whole refetch is impossible is exactly where the innocent one dies permanently. Two consequences: gate the strict rule on a marker THIS code writes so it is absolute only where it is provably right (a10's corollary — a writer that stamps the real length cannot over-stamp), and when local evidence cannot separate the two shapes, ASK THE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the disputed bytes instead of loosening the rule (a bounded read that compares them is positive evidence; a splice scan is only absence of one kind of evidence). The heal that follows must be bounded to the case with no other remedy, paid once, durable the moment it is proven, and its refusals must be remembered in MEMORY — a refusal stamped on disk freezes the corruption in. (a12) A degrade-path log obeys the "say what you swallowed" law AND the "do not say it 500 times" one: rate-limit per host and carry the suppressed count forward — a suppressed fault is not a forgotten fault. (b) Any rewrite a validator performs on a declared path must be a rewrite the consumer performs too; where they differ, refuse rather than emit the wider form (a normalization that widens a grant is a silent privilege escalation). (c) The rule "count only what the USER did" has to enumerate everything that is not the user — one exception (our nudge) is a hint that there are others (a peer message). (d) An in-flight request belongs to the turn that started it: when that turn is cancelled, record the cancellation and DISCARD the answer — never let a round trip that outlived its turn start a billed one.

**Pins.** scripts/test-codex-zst.mjs ⑥c (a buried splice; a magic straddling the 1 MiB chunk boundary; a hybrid that ALREADY carries provenance — refused, because `sameRemote` is not evidence; the one-time cost proven by counting the scan's own reads across two polls; a >1 MiB clean over-cap slot that must still adopt; the ssh rung's stamp AND its delta growth under the cap it was adopted with, plus the live-overtake, short-read and unverifiable-cache negative controls; the honest cap error with a "do exactly what the old text said" control; tiny-transcript short-circuit with two negative controls — every one red with its own fix reverted); ⑥d/⑥e (round 3: a re-compressed .zst remote over a .zst cache refetched WHOLE on BOTH rungs, with the guard-less legality predicate asserted to call that growth legal and the spliced bytes shown to decompress to the OLD transcript — both legs red when the compression clause is deleted from their own rung; a `tail` the host cannot run and a short tail both falling back to the whole cat under the cap, with an over-cap negative control proving the fallback is not a cap bypass; `adopted`/`slab` surviving a delta on both rungs and cleared by a whole refetch); ⑥f/⑥g (rounds 4-5: the two overlapping fetches and the moved offset; then the verifier's dial-transport scenario — slab rung first, ssh rung reachable, remote past the cap, a foreign 203-byte append during `fsReadRange` — refused on BOTH rungs with cache+meta byte-identical, refused AGAIN on the next poll by the stamped-size leg alone, each leg isolated (only the typed verdict removed still refuses, but the caller loses the diagnosis), the pre-fix shape restored by neutering all three legs and shown to seal the corrupt slot and serve it forever, the degrade line asserted verbatim with a healthy-fetch control, and the overtaking whole `cat` stamping what it fetched with a pre-fix-meta control); ⑥h (round 6: an over-cap slot seeded with the old stat-sized meta and a CLEAN longer cache — the pre-fix permanent failure reproduced first (refused twice, nothing can ever move), then healed by one bounded probe of exactly [stamp, file) and grown by the ordinary delta, on the ssh rung AND its slab twin; the heal proven durable across a delta that dies on the wire; a DIRTY longer cache of the same length and with no splice marker refused with the checked-mismatch diagnosis, cache+meta byte-identical, its verdict memoized in memory and re-probed once the memo is cleared; a buried splice marker refused with NO remote read and without claiming the check it skipped; the same shape under the cap refetched whole with no probe at all; a marker-carrying meta refused without asking anyone; a probe that dies on the wire refusing as RETRYABLE and healing on the next poll; and the degrade line rate-limited per host with a second host and a window-expiry leg — ten mutations, each reddening the suite alone); scripts/test-plugin-security.mjs (`~/.*` / `/srv/a/.*` refused, the pre-fix outputs `/home/u*` / `/srv/a*` asserted never produced, `~/.config/*` and `~/./*` unaffected); scripts/test-acp-harness.mjs (the peer entry excluded from the notice, the nudge's silent queue entry, and a Stop held inside a deliberately delayed stop-check with a same-server control that proves the delay itself still nudges).
## THE WRITER SWEEP KILLED READERS, AND ITS TWIN NEVER RAN AT ALL (B-3185, src/writer-sweep.js + src/cli-identity.js + src/server/boot-restore.js + src/hosts.js + src/routes/sessions.js)

Two defects in the same scan, one of them destructive and one of them silently dead.

**(1) A substring decided who dies.** The pre-resume sweep finds processes holding a conversation's transcript open and SIGTERMs the ones that are the agent CLI. "Is it the CLI" was `case "$(ps -p $pid -o args=)" in *claude*)` — a substring over the WHOLE command line — so ANY process whose argv merely NAMED a path under `~/.claude` qualified: `tail -f ~/.claude/projects/<id>.jsonl`, an editor with the transcript open, and a test or agent process running from a git worktree under `~/.claude/worktrees/`, which is where the worktree-only-smokes law puts every agent. The suite hit this first: holding the transcript fd in its own process, it matched its own guard and SIGTERMed itself — exit 143, `npm run ci` red, on code that was fine — and the response at the time was a WORKAROUND IN THE TEST (spawn a holder with a neutral argv) rather than a fix, so the live hazard stayed. Same bug in the codex legs via `*codex*`. Same-origin A/B, identical fixtures, only the script swapped: OLD kills `tail -f` and the worktree process (both `survived=false`); NEW leaves both alive and still kills the real writer.

FIX: `vs_is_cli <pid> <claude|codex>` decides by the EXECUTABLE, in the three rungs that cover the three shapes the CLIs ship in — argv[0]'s basename (native install / vendor binary), the interpreter's FIRST NON-FLAG operand when argv[0] is node/bun/deno (npm shebang shim, `…/claude-code/cli.js`, `…/codex/bin/codex.js`), and `/proc/<pid>/exe` (a native claude execs `~/.local/share/claude/versions/<ver>`). argv comes NUL-split from `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` where it exists, `ps -o args=` elsewhere. A later ARGUMENT never identifies a process. The fd evidence stays the PRIMARY signal — vs_is_cli only answers writer-or-reader — and the codex ARGV leg (`codex resume <tid>` / `CODEX_WEBUI_RESUME_ID=<tid>`) is deliberately exempt because it is self-evidencing and the shape it catches (an orphaned wrapper / its dtach master) is not the codex binary.

**(2) The scan forked per process, and its twin forked per FD.** Measured on the dev box (32 cores, loadavg 3.4–4.8, 3678–3713 processes, 405,735 open fds): the sweep's `ls`+`grep` PAIR per process = 7356 forks and 9.9–12.2 s wall against a 20 s budget — over half of it spent on fork/exec, and past the budget entirely on a busier or bigger machine. boot-restore's "which conversations does a live claude still hold?" probe was the same scan written a second time as a `readlink` fork PER FD — ~6.4 minutes here — against a 6 s timeout, so it ALWAYS timed out, and a bare `catch {}` turned that into "nobody is live": the boot socket dedup silently lost its liveness signal and fell back to createdAt. (Its `/proc/[0-9]*/fd/*` glob was NOT an ARG_MAX case, which is what the first fix's comment claimed and the r2 review corrected: a shell `for` loop expands in the shell's own memory and never reaches execve. ARG_MAX bounds `vs_fd_chunk`, which EXECS `ls` — that is why THAT is chunked.) FIX: ONE shared `fdScanShellFns()` in writer-sweep.js — one `ls -l` per 400 fd directories + one awk, ~20 forks, 3.0–3.5 s — embedded verbatim by both backend scripts and by boot-restore, whose failures now LOG. A/B on the same fixture: old probe `FAILED after 6007ms ETIMEDOUT`, new probe `ok in 3160ms` with the holder named.

**WHAT THE FIELD MEASUREMENT ALSO SAID (do not overclaim this fix).** The installed claude (2.1.226, native) does NOT hold its transcript open — it appends and closes; a machine-wide scan found ZERO holders of any `~/.claude/projects/**.jsonl` with 16 CLIs running. So (i) the claude FD leg mostly finds READERS, not writers — which is exactly why a substring identity test there was dangerous rather than merely sloppy — and the leg that actually reaches a live claude is its own `~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json` lock file (unchanged, now behind the same executable test); (ii) boot-restore's probe is fixed as a MECHANISM (no stall, no silent catch) but still answers "nobody" for current claude, so `claudeAlive` remains effectively false locally. Giving it the CLI registry keyed with `procStart` is the real fix and is deliberately NOT in this commit: retiring is destructive (SIGTERM the owner + unlink the dtach socket), and changing which socket boot destroys is its own decision, not a rider on a performance fix. Read-only field validation of the new predicate against ~3700 live processes: of 70 whose argv merely contains 'claude', exactly the 16 real CLIs answer yes; every dtach master and chat-wrapper that carries the whole `…/claude --resume …` line as ARGUMENTS answers no — the old rule said yes to all of them, and SIGTERMing a dtach master destroys the session (`data/sockets/cw-*` is the danger constant).

**INVARIANTS: (a) Identify a process by its EXECUTABLE — argv[0], the interpreter's first non-flag operand, /proc/<pid>/exe — never by a substring of the whole command line: the transcript path the process is READING is in its argv too, so a substring test cannot separate the writer from every reader of the same file. (b) The evidence that selects a candidate and the test that decides its fate are different questions: keep the fd evidence primary and let the identity test only classify. (c) A guard that kills must be provable with a NEGATIVE control that is not vacuous — assert the reader really has the file open before asserting it survived. (d) When a suite works around a product guard to stay green, the guard is the bug: the workaround is a report, not a fix. (e) A per-item fork inside a /proc walk is a budget bomb — batch it, and size the budget from a MEASUREMENT on a real process table, not from an intuition. (f) A degrade path that can never succeed is indistinguishable from a feature that was never written: a probe that always times out into a bare catch must at minimum SAY SO. (g) When two places run the same scan, they are one implementation with two call sites — the second copy is where the fix does not land.** **R2 REVIEW ROUND — six defects in the fix itself, each now carrying a negative control (the invariants they add): (h) A DRIFT PIN THAT CANNOT MATCH THE DRIFT IS NOT A PIN. The §1 guard against a reintroduced whole-argv identity test was an unsatisfiable regex — it matched neither the verbatim pre-fix line nor any realistic reintroduction, while the kb advertised it. Assert a pin against the EXACT retired shape, then prove it by putting that shape back and watching it go red. (i) A LOOP THAT CARRIES STATE ACROSS ITEMS MUST RESET IT ON EVERY ITEM, NOT ONLY ON THE ONES IT RECOGNISES: the awk pid attribution cleared `p` only on a header matching `/proc/<pid>/fd:`, and `/proc/self/fd` — appended to every chunk on purpose, and the fd table of the `ls` process, which INHERITS the sweeping shell's fds — is exactly the header it does not recognise, so an inherited matching fd was attributed to the chunk's last numeric pid and that innocent process was the SIGTERM target. (j) A COMMENT THAT NAMES THE WRONG MECHANISM IS HOW THE NEXT PERSON REMOVES THE RIGHT GUARD: the chunking was justified as ARG_MAX on a glob that a SHELL for-loop consumed and never execve'd. (k) A NARROWING FIX MUST NOT WIDEN ANYTHING: rung 3 accepted every process whose `/proc/<pid>/exe` lives under the CLI's `versions/` install dir — and the CLI re-execs that same image as its bundled helpers (measured: 2–3 live `ugrep` processes with argv[0] a bare `ugrep` and exe `…/versions/2.1.238`), so a helper holding an inherited transcript fd became a target inside the very fix that stopped killing readers. Rung 3 now also demands the PRESENTATION (argv[0] names the CLI, or argv[0] renamed nothing at all). (l) REPRODUCE THE SHAPE, DO NOT DESCRIBE IT: the suite labelled its own regression leg from `process.argv[1]`, which node absolutises, while the guard reads the command line AS TYPED — it claimed to be running "the real regression shape" for an argv with no `.claude` in it. A copy of the suite now runs from a real `.claude/worktrees/` checkout both absolutely and relatively, with both argvs read out of /proc and asserted. (m) THE STANDING SWEEP IS THE POINT OF (g): hosts.js's remote-discovery CO leg still carried ALL THREE retired shapes (per-process `tr`+`grep` fork pair, per-FD `readlink`, whole-argv identity — 5.02 s / 8068 forks at 4034 processes vs 3.52 s / ~20 forks ported) three commits after the sweep was fixed. Porting it surfaced a live hazard of its own: the leg is the LAST command of the ssh discovery script, `_ssh` REJECTS a non-zero exit, and a `while read` loop exits with its last iteration's status — so a rollout held by a non-CLI process made the whole host's discovery fail into the serve-stale-cache catch. NEVER LET A SCAN'S FINDINGS DECIDE A SCRIPT'S EXIT STATUS.** **R3 REVIEW ROUND — three defects, one of them the twin r2 chose to record instead of kill: (n) A RECORDED TWIN IS STILL A TWIN. r2 left `src/discovery-facts.js` identifying processes by command line (`pidLooksClaude` = `cmdline.includes('claude')`, `isCodexCommandLine` = a whole-argv regex) and wrote the reason down: it labels a card RUNNING, it never SIGTERMs anything. The blast radius really is different — and it was still the wrong call, because a rule with two spellings has two behaviours the moment either is touched AND because the loose spelling was doing its own damage: measured on the dev box, it answered YES for **106 of 4277 processes** against **16 real claude CLIs** (dtach masters, chat-wrappers, the generated `code` editor helper, a zsh shell-snapshot; codex: **30 vs 4**), so a lock file whose pid had been RECYCLED by any of them produced exactly the phantom "running" session the PID-reuse guard exists to prevent. The rule now lives ONCE in `src/cli-identity.js` — `isCliProcess(pid, name)` beside `cliIdentityShellFns()`, dependency-free so the daemon bundle still carries it — and BOTH suites drive the two spellings over the same live pids in the same instant (a one-sided edit is red in test-writer-sweep §6 and in test-discovery-interpret §8). Field check before shipping the narrowing: over 4277 live processes it never answers YES where the old rule said NO, and every real CLI still answers YES. (o) `(deleted)` IS A NORMAL STATE, NOT AN EDGE CASE. The kernel appends ` (deleted)` to `/proc/<pid>/exe` once the image is replaced on disk — which is precisely what `claude` auto-update and `npm i -g @openai/codex` do to LIVE sessions (two of the four agent CLIs running on this box carry the suffix right now). Unstripped, it defeated BOTH executable rungs — basename `claude (deleted)`, and the r2 "nothing renamed" disjunct comparing `2.1.258` against `2.1.258 (deleted)` — so the sweep skipped the ONE process it exists to stop, a mid-update CLI still appending to the transcript, at the moment a double-writer is most likely. **A guard that reads kernel-formatted state must handle every form the kernel emits.** (p) A CONTROL THAT CANNOT REACH THE CODE IT GUARDS IS NOT A CONTROL. The `vs_argv`-silencing leg drove a pid past `pid_max` — for which `[ -r /proc/<pid>/cmdline ]` is FALSE, so it took the `ps` fallback and never reached the redirect the fix silences; it passed identically on the unfixed code. The failure needs `[ -r ]` to PASS and the OPEN to FAIL, which in production is an unschedulable TOCTOU race, so the SHIPPED text now runs with exactly one literal substituted (the /proc root) against a unix SOCKET — access(2) says readable, open(2) says ENXIO, the shell prints the same `cannot open …` — with the verbatim pre-fix spelling as the control. (A directory is the tempting fixture and the wrong one: `O_RDONLY` on a directory SUCCEEDS, so `tr` fails at READ time and its own `2>/dev/null` swallows it either way — a control that passes on both sides, which is the defect being fixed.) (q) THE SHELL THAT RUNS THE TEXT IS NOT `sh`. The identity text is embedded in scripts that reach a machine three ways, and only ONE of them is `sh -c`: the device rung runs `sh -c <script>`, but BOTH ssh rungs — the sweep's fallback (`sweepWriters`) and the discovery CO leg (`hosts.js _ssh`) — hand the script to `ssh host -- <script>`, which the REMOTE USER'S LOGIN SHELL interprets. "POSIX sh" is therefore the floor, not the target. It bit the (o) fix on arrival: in zsh `(…)` is a glob GROUP, so the unquoted `${vs_c_e% (deleted)}` matched " deleted" and stripped NOTHING — the auto-update fix was dead on exactly the hosts whose login shell is zsh (a very common default, this dev box included), and invisible to every `sh -c` test in the suite, all of which stayed green. Quoting the pattern (`${vs_c_e%' (deleted)'}`) makes it literal in every shell (POSIX: quoted characters in the word are not pattern characters; verified dash/bash/busybox/zsh/ksh). **Quote any pattern whose literal characters are special SOMEWHERE, and test embedded shell text under every shell that can interpret it — not just the one your test harness picks.** The gate is functional: the suite drives the SHIPPED text through every login shell present on the box and demands identical verdicts on the `(deleted)` fixtures, with the unquoted spelling as the negative control — it parses and is INDISTINGUISHABLE under `sh`, and diverges only under zsh, which is precisely why the defect survived a suite that only ever ran `sh`.** (r) A BRANCH NO TEST CAN REACH IS A BRANCH THAT DRIFTS. Every consumer of the identity rule has a SECOND body for machines with no /proc (macOS/BSD ssh hosts), reached by `lsof`, and Linux-only suites had never executed either of them — so both quietly kept the rule the rest of B-3185 retired: `src/discovery-facts.js`'s rung gated on `/codex/.test(cmd)` and the `hosts.js` CO leg's `else` on `awk … c ~ /codex/`, i.e. **lsof's COMMAND field**, which is `comm` (the exec'd file's name, truncated, prctl-settable by the process itself) matched as a SUBSTRING — `codex-keeper`, `codexd`, a dtach master renamed after the thread. The shell sweep never had this: it takes `lsof -t` and runs `vs_is_cli` per pid. Worse, r1/r2 emitted the shared shell functions INSIDE the CO leg's `then` block, so on a mac host `vs_is_cli` did not EXIST in the branch that would have called it. And the JS rung carried a second, independent defect that only running it could reveal: `execFileSync` THROWS on a non-zero exit, and `lsof +D <dir>` returns 1 whenever any file under the tree has no open instance — i.e. essentially always (measured on the real `~/.codex/sessions` and on a single-holder fixture: correct `p`/`n` output, EMPTY stderr, status 1), so the catch produced `[]` = "no codex thread is running" and the entire macOS/BSD codex liveness fact was a degradation path that could only degrade — (h)'s always-fails-so-never-written, again, in the one place no test looked. Fixes: emit `-Fpn` and credit the `p` pid through the shared predicate on BOTH sides; hoist the shell function definitions above the `if`; read lsof's STDOUT and treat only a SPAWN-level failure (no lsof, timeout, buffer overflow) as "cannot tell", because a shell has always ignored lsof's status. **An exit code is an error signal only if the program says it is.** The gates make the branch reachable rather than trusting it: the JS rung is NAMED and exported (`listOpenRolloutPathsViaLsof`) and driven against live fixtures with ONE negative control PER defect, and the CO leg's else-branch is driven by substituting ONE literal — the `[ -d /proc/self ]` probe — leaving the loop, the identity test and the trailing `:` exactly as shipped. **THE STANDING SWEEP, RE-MEASURED (r3 — and the answer is not "zero"):** a FOURTH place asks the same question — `src/session-store.js` `isProcessClaude`/`isProcessClaudeAsync`. **r3 RECORDED THIS ONE'S BLAST RADIUS WRONG, and r4 corrected it (see the r4 round below): the pair is not "the LOCAL sweep's PID-reuse fallback behind B-2104's `procStart` match" — that describes only the ASYNC half. The SYNC `isProcessClaude` had exactly one caller, `/api/kill-pid`'s local branch, i.e. it GATED A SIGTERM, which is precisely the class of caller this whole essay is about; the async half is the one behind `procStart`, reached from `isLockClaude` alone, and it only decides whether a card reads RUNNING.** The rule reads `ps -o comm=` (the name of the file that was EXEC'd), i.e. it looks like an EXECUTABLE test rather than the argv substring B-3185 retired; measured over 4277 live processes it and `isCliProcess` answer YES to **the same 16**, with **zero** divergence either way — **but that measurement was of THIS box's process table, not of the rule: `comm` is 15 bytes the process may set for itself (node renames its main thread to `MainThread`, so an npm-installed `node …/claude-code/cli.js` answers NO) and `.includes('claude')` accepts `claude-keeper`; the local install here is native, which is the only reason the two agreed.** Porting the ASYNC half would be a behaviour change to the hot local sweep whose fallback rung is macOS-only (where `isCliProcess` is SYNCHRONOUS — a per-lock blocking fork is the 2.242.0 stall this async family exists to avoid), and the alternative — teaching the shared predicate a `comm` rung so both sides trivially match — WIDENS a kill path (comm is settable by the process itself via prctl) inside a narrowing fix, which is exactly (k). What it gets instead of prose is a live PARITY GATE: scripts/test-local-discovery-device.mjs already asserts "device-facts sweep === local sweep", so the two rungs are compared on every run — and its fixture was corrected from an ARTIFACT (a `#!/bin/sh` script named `claude`: the kernel gives that process argv[0] `/bin/sh` while `comm` stays `claude`, so it passed one rung and failed the other, pinning a disagreement no real install produces — and a wrapper script's lock file names the CHILD's pid anyway) to a real binary named `claude`. **A twin you keep must be a twin a test compares.** **R4 REVIEW ROUND — three defects, and the first one says the standing sweep had been asking too narrow a question: (s) THE RETIRED RULE WAS STILL LIVE ON A KILL PATH NOBODY HAD ENUMERATED. r1–r3 swept "who decides identity?" through the sweep and through discovery, and never asked "who else can SIGTERM a pid?". `hosts.js killRemotePid` — the sidebar's Terminate for a REMOTE discovered session — still ran `case "$(ps -p N -o args=)" in *claude*|*codex*) kill -TERM N`, the verbatim whole-argv substring B-3185 exists to retire, on a path that KILLS, on a machine the user cannot look at: a remote `tail -f ~/.claude/projects/<id>.jsonl`, an editor with the transcript open, a wrapper whose ARGUMENTS name `…/bin/codex`, or a dtach master carrying the whole `claude --resume …` command line (SIGTERMing which DESTROYS the session) all matched — and the route then answered `{success:true}`, so the user was told it worked. Its LOCAL twin in the same route was the other spelling (`ps -o comm=` + `.includes('claude')`) and wrong in the mirror direction: it could not kill an npm-installed CLI at all (comm is `MainThread` — node renames its own main thread; measured live) while accepting anything calling itself `claude-…`. Both now ask THE identity — the remote through a named `killPidShell(pid)` that embeds `cliIdentityShellFns()` verbatim (a host has no checkout) and tests BOTH CLI names, the local through `isCliProcess(pid,'claude'|'codex')` — so `hostId` is a parameter here too, and the sync `isProcessClaude` is DELETED rather than left lying about. The three outcomes (`VS_GONE`/`VS_OK`/`VS_NOTAGENT`) and the `ps`-based existence test are unchanged (`kill -0` would report another user's process as gone). **Enumerate kill paths as kill paths: the sweep is not the only thing in a product that sends a signal.** The rest of the sweep, with reasons, is short and now written down: the codex argv leg (`*codex*resume*<RID>*` / `CODEX_WEBUI_RESUME_ID=<RID>`) is an OWNERSHIP test, not an identity test — it names the exact conversation, which is self-evidencing, and the shape it catches is deliberately not the CLI binary; every other kill in the tree selects by something WE own (our dtach socket path, our own child pid, a plugin's own install root), never by what a command line says. (t) THE SURVIVING TWIN'S RECORD WAS WRONG — corrected above; a twin you keep must be recorded with the radius it actually has, or the next reviewer accepts a kill-path rule on the strength of a discovery-path justification. It is now pinned as discovery-only: one caller (`isLockClaude`, itself reached from ONE place — the lock probe in the discovery scan), asserted by name, and its sync twin asserted GONE. The honest edge: a lock this rung credits WRONGLY still puts that pid on a card, and the sidebar's Terminate hands that pid to `/api/kill-pid` — but the ROUTE re-asks THE identity and refuses, which is precisely why the gate belongs where the SIGTERM is and not on the label that led there. (u) THE TWO SPELLINGS DISAGREED ON A NEWLINE INSIDE AN argv WORD. argv is a list of NUL-separated words; the JS twin reads that list, but the shell turned NULs into newlines and took the Nth LINE — the FIRST LINE of the Nth word. Verified on live processes, in both directions and both harmful: argv[0] `/usr/bin/claude<LF>/usr/bin/tail` is basename `tail` to JS and `claude` to the old shell (the sweep kills a reader), and `<dir>/dir<LF>name/claude` is the reverse (a real writer survives the sweep, and the double-writer corruption happens). The shell now parks real newlines on `\001` across the line select and restores them after, so "the Nth line" IS "the Nth NUL-record" in both spellings, and the `ps` fallback flattens its blob the way the JS twin's `/\s+/` split always did. **AND THAT WAS ONLY HALF OF IT — the round-4 fix was itself measured, and the value still had to survive `$(…)`, which strips EVERY trailing newline.** So a word (or a path) that ENDS in one still read `…/claude` in the shell and `…/claude<LF>` in JS, and the shell's answer is the PERMISSIVE one, on the paths that kill: verified on live processes for all three captures — argv[0] `…/claude<LF>` (rung 1), argv[0] `…/claude<0x01>` (the park byte itself comes back out as a newline, so it was eaten too — the code comment claiming that residue "can only make a word look LESS like the CLI" was false for a TRAILING one), and `/proc/<pid>/exe` `…/claude<LF>` under a launcher argv[0] (rung 3, which no argv fixture can reach). One helper `vs_cap` now captures all three: a sentinel byte appended INSIDE the subshell protects the tail, then exactly ONE terminator — the one the producer itself printed — comes off. **A fix for "the two spellings read this structure differently" is not done until the value has been carried all the way to the comparison: the transport (`$(…)`) mangles it too, and a partial fix leaves the harmful direction alive.** **When one spelling of a rule can read a structure the other cannot, the difference is not academic — it is a different answer on the input that carries the structure.** **R5 REVIEW ROUND — three defects, and two of them are the same shape: a rung the harness cannot reach, and a name in a comment that no longer exists. (v) THE EXISTENCE PROBE IN FRONT OF THE KILL WAS BUSYBOX-BLIND. r4 fixed WHO `killRemotePid` may SIGTERM and left the question BEFORE it — does this pid exist? — spelled `C=$(ps -p N -o args=)`, with the reason written down that `kill -0` would report another user's live process as gone. busybox `ps` has no `-p` at all (measured here, busybox 1.37.0: `ps: invalid option -- 'p'` plus a usage block on stderr, exit 1, stdout EMPTY), and the capture's whole point is `2>/dev/null` — so on a host whose login shell lives in busybox (Alpine images, embedded boxes, any `ash` rootfs, and remember BOTH ssh rungs hand this text to the REMOTE USER'S shell) EVERY Terminate answered `VS_GONE` and the route returned `{success:true, gone:true}` while NOTHING had been signalled: the user was told the process was already gone, the card flipped, and the CLI kept running and kept writing. **A capability the probe does not have must never read as a FACT about the subject.** The fix is a ladder in which every rung is POSITIVE evidence: `kill -0` (POSIX, a shell builtin everywhere — its SUCCESS is proof; r4's objection was only ever about its FAILURE, where EPERM and ESRCH share one exit status, so a failure is handed to the next rung instead of believed), then `[ -d /proc/N ]` (Linux incl. every busybox host, world-visible for a process we may not signal), then `ps -p N` (the no-/proc rung — BSD/macOS `ps` does have `-p`). And a second, quieter lie went with it: once the pid is known to exist, `vs_is_cli` answering NO has two very different causes — we READ its argv/exe and it is a `tail` (a finding), or we could read NEITHER (no /proc AND a `ps` that cannot answer, i.e. exactly the busybox combination). `vs_known` separates them, so the outcomes are FOUR: `VS_GONE` / `VS_OK` / `VS_NOTAGENT` / `VS_UNKNOWN` (alive, no evidence readable), and `killRemotePid` THROWS with an explanation on the last two instead of manufacturing a success. The enumerated sibling `src/server/sysinfo-wiring.js signalProc` keeps its `ps -p`, with the reason re-derived rather than inherited: there it sits on the FAILURE branch of a kill that was already ATTEMPTED, so it can mislabel EPERM as ESRCH but can never report a kill that did not happen as a success — pinned by asserting the `kill` precedes any `ps -p` in its script. (w) THE `ps` FALLBACK RUNG OF THE r4 FIX HAD NEVER BEEN RUN. `vs_argv`'s `else` branch only executes where there is no /proc, r4 changed it (`tr '\n' ' '` before awk) and justified it with a sentence about the JS twin — but every fixture on a Linux box takes the /proc rung, so the claim shipped as prose. It is now driven with NO edit to the text under test, by two environment substitutions that together spell "this machine has no /proc, and its `ps` is not procps": the `/proc/$1/` root is re-rooted (three literals, asserted — re-rooting only the cmdline read leaves rung 3 answering from `/proc/<pid>/exe`, and the `ps` rung never decides anything), and a stand-in `ps` goes first on PATH. The stand-in is asserted to be NECESSARY, not assumed: measured here, procps `ps -o args=` renders an argv word's embedded newline as a SPACE, so this box's own `ps` cannot produce the multi-line blob the flattening exists for — and the branch only ever runs on a platform whose `ps` this box does not have. The JS side is DRIVEN too, not mirrored: a child node process whose two /proc reads throw runs the SHIPPED `procArgv`/`isCliProcess`. Result: the two spellings return the identical word for argv[0..2] and the identical verdict on three live fixtures, and the verbatim pre-r4 line (no flattening — awk then prints field i of EVERY line) answers the OPPOSITE of the JS twin on BOTH newline fixtures while remaining indistinguishable on a plain one. **A rung whose test can only take the other rung is a rung with no test.** (x) A COMMENT ABOUT IDENTITY NAMED A FUNCTION THAT NO LONGER EXISTS. scripts/test-local-discovery-device.mjs — the page that ARGUES why a second spelling of "is this pid claude?" is allowed to survive — still credited the local rung to `isProcessClaude`, the sync twin r4 DELETED, and still glossed `comm` as "the name of the file that was EXEC'd", which r4 had just measured to be false as an identity claim. On that page, of all pages, a stale name is an invitation to re-add the retired rule. Corrected to `isProcessClaudeAsync` reached from `isLockClaude`'s no-`procStart` fallback (which is why that fixture's lock deliberately carries no numeric `procStart`), and the note now carries a DRIFT GUARD: every identity function it names must be DEFINED in one of the three modules it attributes them to, and the deleted sync twin must be nameable nowhere — not in the note, not in session-store's code — with the verbatim pre-r5 sentence as the negative control. **Documentation that justifies keeping a twin is load-bearing: guard its names the way the code's names are guarded.** **R6 REVIEW ROUND — one defect, and it is r5's own escape hatch: (y) THE ENUMERATED SIBLING WAS NOT SAFE, AND THE REASON THAT SAID SO ONLY DESCRIBED HALF OF IT. r5 fixed `hosts.js killPidShell`, ENUMERATED `src/server/sysinfo-wiring.js signalProc` as the other kill path, and let it keep its `ps -p` on a hand-written reason: 'there it sits on the FAILURE branch of a kill that was already ATTEMPTED, so it can mislabel EPERM as ESRCH but can never report a kill that did not happen as a success' — pinned by asserting the `kill` precedes any `ps -p`. That script has TWO `ps -p` calls and the sentence is true of the SECOND only. The FIRST is the post-signal aliveness check on the SUCCESS branch, and there a busybox-blind probe does not mislabel an outcome, it MANUFACTURES one: measured here (busybox 1.37.0; fixture `trap \"\" TERM; sleep 60`) the pre-r6 script answers `OK-GONE` for a process that is still running, so `signalProc` returns `{ok:true, gone:true}` — the process-manager row flips to gone, the user believes the Terminate worked, and the CLI keeps writing. The failure branch's mislabel is real too and also measured: a live pid this uid may not signal answered `ESRCH` = 'no such process (already gone)' rather than EPERM. **A twin kept alive by a comment is a twin, and the comment is only as good as its author's count of the call sites** — the ordering pin was satisfiable and true and still let the defect through, because it asked about ORDER when the question was CAPABILITY. The fix is therefore not a second, better reason: `vs_alive` moved into src/cli-identity.js beside the identity text (same three transports, same remote-login-shell floor, dependency-free so the daemon still bundles it) and BOTH scripts embed it, so no per-site judgement remains to be got wrong; `signalVerdictScript(pid, sig)` is module-level and EXPORTED so the suite drives the shipped bytes and validates pid/signal AT the builder. And the class gets a STANDING SWEEP rather than a memory: no `ps -p` may serve as an EXISTENCE test anywhere on a kill/signal path (cli-identity, writer-sweep, hosts, sysinfo-wiring, session-store, routes/sessions, the agentd installer, every tracked data/bin twin), every surviving occurrence is listed WITH its reason — all of them ARGV/environ READS whose existence question was already settled by `kill -0`, plus the one no-/proc rung inside `vs_alive` itself — and a DEAD allowlist entry fails the suite too, because an exemption nobody prunes is exactly how this one survived a round of review. Honest edge, pinned: a ZOMBIE reads ALIVE to the ladder, to procps `ps -p` and to the local branch's `process.kill(pid,0)` alike — unchanged, kernel-level, and the reason §17's fixtures are double-forked orphans.** **R7 REVIEW ROUND — one defect, and it is the instrument rather than the rule: THE STANDING SWEEP WAS GATED ON A HAND-WRITTEN LIST.** r6 replaced "a twin kept alive by a comment" with a sweep, and then handed that sweep a literal array of seven files (plus `git ls-files data/bin`). A hand list is the SAME instrument this bug has already defeated three times — r4 found the retired rule alive on a kill path nobody had counted, r5 counted the sibling and let it go, r6 found that r5's reason for letting it go described only the second of that script's two `ps -p` calls — so "no `ps -p` existence test on ANY kill/signal path" was enforced exactly where its author had already looked. Measured: the r6 list missed **47** files that really do send or probe a signal, among them `server.js` (it wires signalProc), `src/jobs.js` (verified handle-kills), `src/server/boot-restore.js` (dtach retire = SIGTERM + unlink), `src/plugins.js` / `src/vnc.js` / `src/port-forward.js` / `src/opencode-serve.js` (each stops a daemon it started), `src/agentd/agentd.js` (device-side session pipes) and `src/ws-handler.js` / `src/ws-create.js` (the kill + teardown cases) — every one a place the next probe could land without reddening a thing, and the sweep would still have printed ALL PASS. The fix is that the file set is DERIVED by grep from the question the rule is about: every non-test file under `src/`, `data/bin/` and `scripts/`, plus the repo-ROOT scripts where `server.js` lives, whose text sends or probes a signal (`kill -TERM/-9/-0/…`, `SIG*`, `pkill`, `process.kill(`, `killRemotePid`, `signalProc`, `vs_alive`); extension-less files enter by SHEBANG, which is also how a GENERATED agent CLI (`vibespace-status` is deliberately untracked) is reached at all — `git ls-files data/bin` could never see it. The derived list is PRINTED by the suite, so the reviewer reads what was swept instead of a comment's count of it, and the grep is deliberately OVER-inclusive (the i18n dictionaries match the word `SIGSTOP`, the adapters match `SIGINT`): a false positive only widens where the rule is enforced, a false negative is the whole defect. Two structural pins keep the instrument honest — the derivation must lose nothing the r6 hand list covered (this reddens if the walk roots are narrowed) and it must still cover the ten named permanent kill paths the hand list missed (this reddens if anyone re-narrows to a hand list). And because a sweep only ever run against a clean tree is a sweep proven to say nothing, the SHIPPED sweep is parameterised by ROOT and run a second time against a temp tree built to contain each shape: the retired `ps -p N >/dev/null 2>&1` probe on a brand-new kill path IS caught; an ALLOWLISTED line copied into another file is still stray (the exemption is per file, it does not travel with the text); a kill path with no `ps -p` is swept and stays green; a `ps -p` in a file that signals nothing is out of scope, stated rather than assumed; the suites are excluded, which is the only reason this file may write the retired shape down as a control; and a shebang tool under `data/bin` is caught. A last leg closes the one hole a source scan structurally cannot see: every exported shell BUILDER (`pidAliveShellFn`, `cliIdentityShellFns`, `fdScanShellFns`, `writerSweepScript` claude+codex, `killPidShell`, `codexOpenRolloutsShell`, `signalVerdictScript`) is swept on the text it EMITS, with the verbatim pre-r6 script as that scanner's negative control.  A rebuilt tree caught a real hole in the first cut of this leg: `data/bin/vibespace-agentd.js` is the esbuild bundle of `src/agentd/**`, so it carries cli-identity's and writer-sweep's `ps -p` lines VERBATIM under a filename no per-file allowlist can ever hold — the sweep went red on a CLEAN tree the moment anyone ran `npm run build` (measured). GENERATED files (gitignored = not part of the shipped source) are therefore a THIRD bucket rather than a skip or an allowlist row, and their rule is stricter and needs no author: every `ps -p` line in them must appear VERBATIM in an AUTHORED file the sweep already walked, so a build step cannot introduce a probe and the reason still lives with the author (controls both ways: a bundle that only COPIES an authored probe passes; the same bundle with one line its sources never contained is caught). **The invariant: a standing sweep is only as good as the set it walks — derive the set from the property, never enumerate it, and print what was walked.** Suite: scripts/test-writer-sweep.mjs (240) — writers swept / readers survived incl. the suite's own process under a SIGTERM trap and two copies of it run from a `.claude/worktrees/` checkout, the rung-3 identity matrix (one binary, three argv[0]s) with r1's rung reverted against the live helper as the control, the awk attribution probe with the sticky-`p` revert as the control, the discovery-twin legs (structural + functional + exit status), the two `(deleted)`-image writers (one per exe rung) with the strip reverted as the control, the cross-login-shell verdict parity (dash/bash/busybox/zsh/ksh) with the UNQUOTED `(deleted)` pattern as the control, the JS⇄shell identity parity matrix and the retired JS rule as ITS control, the `vs_argv` silencing control on a socket, the two newline-in-argv[0] fixtures (one per direction) with the pre-r4 `vs_argv` reader as the control, the three TRAILING-byte fixtures (argv[0] in LF, argv[0] in `\001`, an exe PATH in LF) with the three pre-`vs_cap` `$(…)` captures as the control — reverted in the product, five asserts go red including the 46-pair live parity matrix, §14's KILL-PATH legs — the real `killPidShell` text run against real processes (a `tail -f` on a claude transcript and on a codex rollout REFUSED and alive, a real `claude` and a real `codex` terminated, `VS_GONE`, a non-integer pid rejected at the builder) with the verbatim pre-r4 remote line KILLING its own victim as the control, `killRemotePid` ITSELF with the device link stubbed to run the script locally (a builder referenced as a free identifier throws only when the METHOD runs — the lost-binding class no structural pin can see), plus `/api/kill-pid` driven through the real express router (the reader refused 400 and alive; the npm-shape CLI the comm rule could never see terminated) with the retired comm rule as ITS control — the structural pins (one /proc walk, no per-process ls, no whole-argv test, every `kill -TERM` line carries `SWEPT:`, killRemotePid builds from killPidShell, the surviving comm twin has exactly one caller and no sync twin) proven by reintroducing each retired shape, the boot-restore wiring pin, and a self-checking pin on this very number — plus §15's no-/proc `ps`-rung parity (re-rooted /proc + a stand-in `ps`, the JS twin driven into its own fallback in a child, the pre-r4 line as the control) and §16's busybox kill-path legs (the pre-r5 script answering VS_GONE for a live reader AND a live `claude` under busybox as the control, the shipped script refusing/terminating/reporting-gone correctly there, VS_UNKNOWN reached by re-rooting /proc, the caller's four outcomes, and the enumerated `signalProc` sibling, whose pin r6 replaced with the shared-text one) — plus §17's SIGNAL-verdict legs: the measured busybox blindness of the quiet `ps -p N >/dev/null` form, the verbatim pre-r6 script answering OK-GONE for a LIVE `trap "" TERM` process as the control, the shipped builder answering OK-ALIVE on that same process and OK-GONE on one that really dies (fully reaped, asserted via /proc, which is why the fixtures are double-forked orphans), ESRCH for a pid that was never there, a REAL EPERM leg on a live pid this uid may not signal with the pre-r6 ESRCH as its control (skipped-with-a-reason where the environment cannot produce one), signalProc's own four-verdict mapping through a stubbed device link, the builder's pid/signal validation, and the STANDING SWEEP over every kill/signal-path file with its reasoned allowlist. Revert-verified: putting the pre-r6 probe back in the product turns 5 asserts red (naming both offending lines by file:line), a brand-new `ps -p` existence test elsewhere turns the sweep red on its own, and a STALE allowlist entry turns two red. r7 revert-verified the same way: reverting the derivation to the r6 hand list turns the regression pin red (it names the 47 files that fall out), and each of the six temp-root controls is a live measurement of the shipped sweep rather than a description of it. test-local-discovery-device is 9 (the three new asserts are the note's drift guard); test-sysinfo-op is 29 (its two "probe existence via ps -p" pins became three: no bare `kill -0` split, no bare `ps -p <pid>`, and the shared ladder embedded verbatim).

**ROUND 2 — three defects an adversarial verifier reproduced against that fix, and the deeper one the reproduction exposed.**

1. **The MAJOR (its own scenario).** Round 1 keyed the inherited bubble on its CONTENT so codex's copy would collapse onto it — so two INHERITED items with the SAME text steered into one turn were two bubbles live and ONE after a reload. A steered message deleted, live and reload disagreeing, in the exact case the fix exists for ('continue', 'go on', identical agent-to-agent notices — a 25-item queue makes that ordinary).
2. **Measuring it turned up the pre-existing twin.** Codex's OWN user records were content-keyed too. On the OWNER'S rollout — the session in the report — a reload rendered **68 of its 95 user messages: 27 deleted**; across the local corpus, **133 deleted over 89 rollouts**. Every single collision carried a different `msg_…` id AND a different `create_time` (0 same-id, 0 same-create_time): distinct submissions, minutes apart, not one genuine duplicate among them.
3. **A phantom spinner (minor).** The inherited bubble deliberately skips `_finalizeStreaming` (it lands mid-turn), but it was still a hard `break` in that function's backward scan — so a reply left open when the turn ended stayed `status:'streaming'` forever on every rebuild: a spinner on a dead, read-only conversation. The same mechanism the peer-card exemption on that line was written for.
4. **A claim that leaks deletes (minor).** A twin claim short-circuited by the fingerprint's duplicate check was never retired, and the leaked claim later ate a legitimate codex-only record — the deletion the forward-only rule exists to prevent, arriving through the back door.

**THE ROUND-2 RULE: a user submission's identity is the ID its producer minted, never its text.** Ours is keyed by `userRecordIdentity` (webui_msg_id / client_msg_id / **webui_queue_id** — the cid a previous wrapper minted names the same submission, so one namespace), codex's by `codexRecordIdentity` (`msg_…`, its own namespace). Records with no id on either side (pre-0.15x rollouts: 144/572 in the corpus, all ≤2026-05, no file mixed) keep the content key — but ours and codex's stay in SEPARATE content namespaces, so the duplicate check can only ever collapse ONE producer's own record, which is what makes "a record dropped as a duplicate already had its twin effect applied" true and the leak in (4) structurally impossible. The ours↔codex pair is retired by the CLAIM alone, and now EVERY copy of ours claims (round 1 claimed only the id-keyed ones because a content-keyed copy of ours collided with codex's on the fingerprint; that collision is gone).

**AND THE ASYMMETRY THE CLAIM CANNOT COVER.** A forward claim assumes ours is written first. Two producers of ours are written LAST: the `item/completed` twin for an item the app-server DRAINED (it emits that only after persisting its own record) and the IDLE peer path (`turn/start` commits before `recordPeerMessage` runs — test-peer-msg-card had pinned exactly that order since 2.362.2 and caught the first, provenance-blind attempt at this rule). Such a record marks itself `webui_after_commit` and YIELDS to an unconsumed codex copy of the same content **in the same turn** — it drops ITSELF, never deletes anything — while an early copy never yields, so a same-text neighbour can never swallow one. `webui_queue_via` ('steered'|'drained') stays as forensics; the READER reads the commit-order fact only, because reading the queue label would have made the rule queue-only.

**ROUND-2 INVARIANTS.** (f) **Identity before content**: keying a record by what it SAYS collapses distinct facts — the corpus number (133 + 27 real deletions) is what that costs. (g) **A duplicate is only a duplicate within one producer**: two producers' records must never share a key namespace, or the dedupe silently means two different things. (h) **A message that does not CLOSE a turn's open streams must not HIDE them either** — the exemption is the same one, on both sides of that scan. (i) **Every claim must be retired on every path that drops the record standing for it**, including the duplicate short-circuit; an unretired claim is a deletion waiting for the same text to appear again. (j) **A producer that writes after the commit must SAY so**: the wrapper's three writers of a user record are now a census the suite counts, and a fourth answers "had the app-server committed it yet?" before it ships. (k) A negative control is a PATCHED COPY of the real module (asserted to have matched), never a hand-written imitation of what I believe the old code did.
